title: When appetite must answer to the wealth that travels
issueStatement: Greed often arrives dressed as prudence: one more purchase, one more reserve, one more advantage before the hand can rest. Gurbani names the cost plainly—the heart becomes crowded with tastes while Naam is pushed out of its dwelling.
centralInsight: The Guru changes the question from what can be gained to what can be carried. False trade makes the mind and body false; praise, truthful labor, sharing, and Naam become the wealth that leaves the soul lighter rather than trapped.
practicalReflection: Greed is not cured by despising things. It is weakened when the next desire is brought before the Door and asked whether it makes room for Naam, honest work, and an open hand.
actionPrompt: Before taking more, name the fear underneath the wanting and choose one concrete act of praise, restraint, or sharing that lets Naam keep room in the heart.
searchTerms: training desire to live inside enough

source.shortMeaning: Greed is exposed as a degrading appetite when it crowds the mouth with falsehood, slander, anger, and self-praise instead of speech that can stand at the Lord’s Door.
source.lifeApplication: When wanting rises, pause before it reaches the tongue or the hand; ask whether this desire would leave you honorable before the One who judges the heart.

excerpts.explanation: The overview begins with the shabad’s fierce diagnosis of greed as a dog and appetite as a crowd of tastes that leaves little room for Naam.

source.shortMeaning: The shabad turns buying and profit toward the soul, insisting that only praise, truth, and Naam travel beyond false dealing.
source.lifeApplication: Before the next acquisition or status move, ask whether it adds truth to the heart or only more weight for the mind to carry.

excerpts.explanation: This source gives greed a mercantile test: buy only what the All-knowing Merchant can receive and care for.

source.shortMeaning: The outstretched hand that begs for riches is answered by the Gurmukh who keeps the Lord clasped to the heart and is kept close like a cherished servant.
source.lifeApplication: Let one grasping impulse become a return to remembrance; keep the Lord close before asking the world to make you safe.

excerpts.explanation: This passage contrasts the begging hand of craving with the closeness given to the humble servant held by the Lord.

daily.label: Daily
daily.title: When a small wanting starts crowding Naam out
daily.issueStatement: A normal day can be bent by a quiet reach: the tab left open, the comparison checked again, the extra thing justified as harmless. The shabad refuses to call this neutral when the heart is being trained by appetite.
daily.centralInsight: Greed is not only the size of the desire; it is the way desire begins to occupy the mouth, the imagination, and the next choice. Gurbani brings the ordinary reach back under the question of honor at the Lord’s Door.
daily.practicalReflection: The daily correction is early and small. Stop the wanting before it becomes the mood of the hour, and give the heart a word of praise or a generous act instead.
daily.actionPrompt: Today, when a small wanting asks to lead, pause for one breath of Naam and leave one needless thing untaken, unclicked, or unspoken.

source.shortMeaning: Greed, falsehood, slander, anger, and self-praise are named as degrading appetites before the shabad asks for speech worthy of honor.
source.lifeApplication: Interrupt the small wanting before it shapes the mouth; choose the word or silence that could stand at the Lord’s Door.

excerpts.explanation: Daily greed is grounded here in the shabad’s concrete images of appetite entering speech and conduct.

source.shortMeaning: The path is recognized in honest labor and an open hand, not in religious posture that keeps taking while pretending holiness.
source.lifeApplication: Make one ordinary exchange cleaner today: earn honestly, pay fairly, and give something from your hand.

excerpts.explanation: This source turns the ordinary day away from grasping by joining work with generosity.

source.shortMeaning: True wealth belongs to those who trade in Naam and listen until patience, honor, and glory ripen.
source.lifeApplication: Let one impulse wait long enough for remembrance to become the first wealth you touch.

excerpts.explanation: This passage gives the day a different economy: listening to Naam instead of obeying appetite.

pressure.label: Under Pressure
pressure.title: When scarcity makes grasping sound responsible
pressure.issueStatement: Under strain, greed rarely announces itself as greed. It speaks as security, timing, leverage, or survival, and the tight room starts blessing whatever keeps the self in control.
pressure.centralInsight: Gurbani answers pressure by asking what survives the pressure. The object worth buying is the one that goes with the soul; the true merchandise is praise carried with focused consciousness.
pressure.practicalReflection: Pressure tempts the heart to call possession safety. The shabad moves safety toward praise, Sangat, Naam, and receiving what the Creator gives instead of taking control by force.
pressure.actionPrompt: When scarcity tightens the room, delay the grasping move and ask: will this carry praise forward, or only teach fear to make my decisions?

source.shortMeaning: Only the object that travels with the soul is worth buying; the real merchandise is the Lord’s praise carried with focused consciousness.
source.lifeApplication: When pressure says to secure more, ask whether the move can be carried before the All-knowing Merchant.

excerpts.explanation: This source directly tests pressure’s urgency against what endures beyond the moment.

source.shortMeaning: Human birth is a chance to meet the Lord, not a season to spend on useless pursuits in Maya.
source.lifeApplication: Let urgency send you to Sangat and Naam rather than another anxious acquisition.

excerpts.explanation: This passage refuses to let strain make greed look like the most important work of a rare life.

source.shortMeaning: Receiving itself stands under the Lord’s pleasure; mercy gives the jewel of Naam where self-willed grasping would lose it.
source.lifeApplication: Practice receiving what is given before reaching for what fear demands.

excerpts.explanation: Pressure loosens here because the heart is placed under Hukam rather than under scarcity’s command.

repair.label: After the Slip
repair.title: When the grasping has already taken more than love allowed
repair.issueStatement: After greed acts, the heart wants either excuse or disgust. Gurbani gives a cleaner repair: admit the appetite, see the false trade, and turn the hand back toward Naam and conduct that can bear honor.
repair.centralInsight: Repair begins when greed is named without ornament. The shabad calls it degrading, shows how false dealing makes the whole person false, and still points the mind back to praise through the Guru’s Word.
repair.practicalReflection: Do not make the slip your identity, but do not protect it either. Return what can be returned, tell the truth where harm was hidden, and let one act of generosity answer the grasping.
repair.actionPrompt: After the grasping is visible, make one repair before the day closes: return, confess, give, or simplify in the exact place appetite overreached.

source.shortMeaning: Greed is named as a degrading appetite alongside falsehood, slander, anger, and self-praise, then answered by speech that brings honor.
source.lifeApplication: Let repair begin with plain naming; refuse the sentence that makes greed sound noble.

excerpts.explanation: After a slip, this source keeps the heart from sanitizing what actually happened.

source.shortMeaning: All receiving stands under the Lord’s pleasure, and the Naam is obtained by mercy rather than self-willed control.
source.lifeApplication: Bring the overreach back under Hukam; receive the chance to repair instead of tightening around shame.

excerpts.explanation: This passage prevents repair from becoming self-punishment by placing return inside divine giving and mercy.

source.shortMeaning: The highest practice joins Naam to pure conduct, Sangat that washes the dirty mind, and speech sweetened by remembrance.
source.lifeApplication: Make the repair visible in conduct, not only in feeling sorry.

excerpts.explanation: This source gives the grasping heart a concrete way back through clean conduct, company, and speech.

evidence.coreClaim: Repair begins when greed is named without ornament. The shabad calls it degrading, shows how false dealing makes the whole person false, and still points the mind back to praise through the Guru’s Word.
evidence.turn: After greed acts, the heart wants either excuse or disgust. Gurbani gives a cleaner repair: admit the appetite, see the false trade, and turn the hand back toward Naam and conduct that can bear honor.

practice.label: Steady Practice
practice.title: When desire needs a seven-day trade in true wealth
practice.issueStatement: Greed weakens slowly when the heart is given a better trade to repeat. The practice is not vague restraint; it is buying what goes with the soul until the body learns that not every appetite deserves obedience.
practice.centralInsight: The Guru’s economy is concrete: praise as merchandise, truth as assets, Naam as wealth, and the humble servant kept close. Repetition trains desire to ask for what lightens the soul instead of what loads it with doubt.
practice.practicalReflection: A kept practice turns enoughness from an idea into a reflex. The same cue, held for several days, gives desire a smaller throne and gives remembrance more room.
practice.actionPrompt: For seven days, choose one recurring cue for wanting; at that cue, recite one line of praise and move one resource—money, time, attention, or food—toward generosity.

source.shortMeaning: False dealing burdens the mind and body, while praise, truth, and Naam are the wealth the All-knowing Merchant receives.
source.lifeApplication: Use the same daily cue to ask whether this trade adds truth or only weight.

excerpts.explanation: This source supplies the practice’s central image: repeated buying of what can travel with the soul.

source.shortMeaning: The true bankers trade in the Lord’s Name, and patience, honor, and glory ripen from listening to Naam.
source.lifeApplication: Let repetition teach the heart to wait long enough for Naam to become wealth.

excerpts.explanation: This passage makes restraint positive by naming patience and honor as fruit of trading in Naam.

source.shortMeaning: The Gurmukh keeps the Lord clasped to the heart and is kept close by the Lord like a cherished servant.
source.lifeApplication: Let each repeated refusal of excess become a way of keeping the Lord close.

excerpts.explanation: Practice becomes tender here, not merely austere, because desire is answered by closeness to the One who cherishes the humble.
